one_liner: Rust command-line filter that drops duplicate lines with a hash set, replacing sort -u and sort | uniq -c when order does not matter.
what_it_does: huniq reads records from stdin (newline by default, -d DELIM or -0 for NUL) and prints each distinct record the first time it appears, keeping input order; huniq -c prints 'count record' for every distinct record in arbitrary order, and -s/-S sort that report by count. It is a separate CLI with its own flags, not a drop-in for uniq: it never sorts the records themselves and needs no sorted input.
how_it_is_fast: It replaces the O(n log n) sort that `sort -u` and `sort | uniq -c` need with a single pass over a hash table (hashing instead of sorting). In uniq mode it stores only a 64-bit aHash of each distinct record in a std HashSet keyed through an identity hasher, so memory grows with the number of distinct records, not their length; input is split with bstr's for_byte_record_with_terminator (memchr), and the set is leaked with mem::forget at exit instead of being freed. Count mode keeps every distinct record as a Vec<u8> in an aHash HashMap.
when_to_use: Deduplicating log lines, URLs, IDs or word lists in a shell pipeline where first-occurrence order is fine or preferred, and you would otherwise run sort -u.
Streaming dedupe of a live feed (tail -f | huniq): each new distinct line is written as soon as it is seen.
Frequency reports with huniq -c or -cS when sorted keys are not needed, and the distinct set fits in RAM (the README shows about 132 MB for /usr/share/dict/* in -c mode).
Inputs with long records and moderate cardinality: uniq mode holds 8 bytes of hash per distinct record regardless of record length.
when_not_to_use: You need sorted output or uniq -c's padded format: output is in input order (uniq) or random order (-c), and the -c format is 'count record' without padding (open issue #30).

Short numeric keys: in issue #25 a hyperfine run on 1M seq lines measured awk '!a[$0]++' at 281.9 ms vs huniq 407.4 ms, and on 60M lines huniq was only about 2 s faster than awk (30 s vs 32 s); the maintainer says numeric keys are not a case huniq optimizes for.

Very large files where speed matters most: cuniq's PERFORMANCE.md measured huniq 2.7.0 at 6m04.6s vs cuniq --memmap --threads=1 at 2m47.5s on the same 32 GiB file; huniq is single-threaded with no memory-mapped input.
Distinct sets larger than RAM: unlike GNU sort it never spills to disk, and -c keeps every distinct record in memory.
Workloads that cannot tolerate a silently dropped distinct line: uniq mode compares 64-bit hashes only.

integration.platforms: any Rust target; no prebuilt binaries (GitHub releases and a musl binary are requested in open issues #23 and #21)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces `sort -u` and `sort | uniq -c` only when sorted output is not required; flags and -c output format differ from GNU uniq.

gotchas: Correctness bug behind the published numbers: the README tables are the first pass of benchmark_results.txt, last changed in commit 78a0680 'Release 2.1.0' (2020-01-19). In 2.1.0, uniq mode hashed each line with C xxHash's XXH3_64bits_withSecret (vendored, called through bindgen FFI) using `let mut secret = [0u8, 8];`, a 2-byte array instead of 8 bytes, while xxHash requires at least XXH3_SECRET_SIZE_MIN = 136 bytes; every hash therefore read stack memory past the array (an out-of-bounds read in the hot path). Commit f3c1eb0 ('Fix secret... Should be 32 byte', 2.2.1, 2020-05-13) changed it to [0u8; 32], still below 136; aHash replaced it in 2.4. benchmark.sh sends every output to /dev/null and never checks it, so whether 2.1.0 removed duplicates correctly was not verified.

Uniq mode keeps only a 64-bit aHash per distinct record with a per-process random seed, so a collision silently drops a distinct line and differs from run to run (about a 2.7% chance of at least one collision at 1e9 distinct lines, derived from the birthday bound). The author's C++ v1 used 128-bit MetroHash because 'It has to be 128 bits because of the birthday problem.'

Errors are printed with println! to stdout and the process exits 0; when the reader closes the pipe early (huniq | head) it panics with 'failed printing to stdout: Broken pipe (os error 32)' (open issue #32, also #26).

Since commit c51e62c (2.2) removed the BufWriter, output goes through Rust's StdoutLock, which std always wraps in a LineWriter, so every newline-terminated output record is its own write(2) call; the README timings were taken with 2.1.0's BufWriter. Count mode also allocates a fresh Vec<u8> for every input line (BufRead::split) and its output order changes between runs.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick huniq over cuniq when you want the deduplicated lines themselves, streamed in first-occurrence order, rather than a count or report; cuniq was 2.2x faster on the 32 GiB count test and adds memory-mapped, multithreaded and HyperLogLog modes. Over runiq it is the simpler choice and was faster in both third-party tables (6m04.6s vs runiq --filter=quick 7m19.4s); hist-rs fits better when you want a count-sorted histogram.
verified_claims_summary: Author-run in January 2020 on an unstated machine with unstated compiler and tool versions: huniq 2.1.0 (no LTO, C xxHash for uniq mode) against the author's C++ v1 (-O3, synced iostreams, tsl::sparse_set of 128-bit MetroHash), awk, datamash and GNU sort -u in the default locale, on /usr/share/dict/* repeated 1-100 times. The README shows 0.26 s vs 1.67 s (C++) and 7.30 s (sort -u) at 1 repetition and 43.65 vs 154.99 vs 1062.07 s at 100, but the second pass in benchmark_results.txt gives 0.38 vs 2.39 vs 10.40 s and 32.65 vs 130.76 s (4.0x vs C++), so cells move by up to 46% between passes. A competitor's run (cuniq PERFORMANCE.md, Ryzen 7 7800X3D, Windows 11, 32 GiB with 6.03 billion lines) gives a more modest current figure: huniq 2.7.0 6m04.6s vs GNU sort -u 8.32 (8 threads) 14m11.9s (2.3x) and huniq -c 9m32.0s vs sort | uniq -c 28m46.8s (3.0x, derived from page data).
status_note: Stale: last release 2.7.0 on 2022-04-20 and last commit 2024-01-26 (a trivial trim_end change), with the broken-pipe panic still open; BSD-3-Clause per Cargo.toml and the readme text (GitHub detects no LICENSE file), one 217-line Rust file and easy to vendor; 265 stars and 355,150 crates.io downloads; the README benchmark measured 2.1.0, whose hash call had an out-of-bounds read, and has not been re-run since.
